docs.title: Overview
docs.text: hya is a library of custom OmegaConf resolvers designed to be used with Hydra. A resolver is a function that a configuration calls with the syntax ${key:argument,...}. With hya, a configuration can compute values (arithmetic and math functions), build paths and identifiers, and create NumPy arrays or PyTorch tensors, instead of repeating hand-computed values.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. import hya registers the resolvers with OmegaConf. No other call is needed.
  2. A configuration calls a resolver by its key, which starts with hya..
  3. OmegaConf calls the resolver when the value is accessed, with the referenced values of the configuration as arguments.

The required dependency is omegaconf. A few resolvers need an optional package (NumPy, PyTorch or braceexpand), which is imported only when one of them is called.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
Install the library:

pip install hya

Then import hya and use the resolvers in a configuration:

import hya
from omegaconf import OmegaConf

# Use resolvers in your configuration
conf = OmegaConf.create(
    {
        "batch_size": 32,
        "num_samples": 1000,
        "num_batches": "${hya.ceildiv:${num_samples},${batch_size}}",
        "learning_rate": "${hya.pow:10,-3}",  # 0.001
    }
)

print(conf.num_batches)  # Output: 32
print(conf.learning_rate)  # Output: 0.001

docs.title: Using with Hydra
docs.text:
Create a configuration file config.yaml:

model:
  input_dim: 784
  hidden_dim: 256
  output_dim: 10

training:
  batch_size: 32
  num_epochs: 10
  learning_rate: ${hya.pow:10,-3} # 0.001

paths:
  data_dir: ${hya.path:/data}
  model_dir: ${hya.iter_join:[${paths.data_dir},models,v1],/}

experiment:
  name: mnist_classifier
  id: ${hya.sha256:${experiment.name}}

Then use it in your Python script:

import hya
import hydra
from omegaconf import DictConfig


@hydra.main(version_base=None, config_path=".", config_name="config")
def main(cfg: DictConfig):
    print(f"Learning rate: {cfg.training.learning_rate}")
    print(f"Model dir: {cfg.paths.model_dir}")
    print(f"Experiment ID: {cfg.experiment.id}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

See Using with Hydra for multiple configuration files, command line overrides and the supported Python versions.

docs.title: Registering Custom Resolvers
docs.text:
You can extend hya with your own resolvers:

from hya import get_default_registry
from omegaconf import OmegaConf

registry = get_default_registry()


@registry.register("multiply")
def multiply_resolver(x, y):
    return x * y


# Register the custom resolver with OmegaConf
registry.register_resolvers()

# Now use it in your configuration
conf = OmegaConf.create({"result": "${multiply:5,3}"})
print(conf.result)  # Output: 15

See Custom Resolvers to override, load lazily and test your resolvers.

docs.title: API stability
docs.text: While hya is in development stage, no API is guaranteed to be stable from one release to the next. In fact, it is very likely that the API will change multiple times before a stable 1.0.0 release. In practice, this means that upgrading hya to a new version will possibly break any code that was using the old version of hya.

docs.title: Custom Resolvers
docs.text: A ResolverRegistry is a map from a key to a resolver. Using a resolver of your own takes two steps: register adds it to a registry, and register_resolvers publishes the registry to OmegaConf. The default registry, returned by get_default_registry(), holds the resolvers of hya. The signatures are in the reference.

docs.title: Creating and Registering Resolvers
docs.text:
You can extend hya with your own custom resolvers:

from hya import get_default_registry

# Get the default registry
registry = get_default_registry()


# Register a simple custom resolver
@registry.register("double")
def double_resolver(x):
    """Double the input value."""
    return x * 2


# Register a more complex resolver
@registry.register("clip")
def clip_resolver(value, min_val, max_val):
    """Clip a value between min and max."""
    return max(min_val, min(value, max_val))


# Register custom resolvers with OmegaConf
# Note: Default hya resolvers are already registered on import
# This only registers your custom resolvers added to the default registry
registry.register_resolvers()

Now use them in your configuration:

hyperparameters:
  base_lr: 0.001
  scaled_lr: ${double:${hyperparameters.base_lr}}

  dropout: 0.7
  clipped_dropout: ${clip:${hyperparameters.dropout},0.0,0.5}

A key is made of names joined by dots (double, my.clip_2), where a name is made of ASCII letters, digits and _ and does not start with a digit. Any other key, such as my-clip, raises a ValueError when it is registered, and a resolver that is not callable raises a TypeError. The decorator needs the key: @registry.register alone raises a TypeError.

docs.title: Overriding Existing Resolvers
docs.text:
You can override a resolver of the registry with the keyword-only exist_ok parameter. The default resolvers are already published to OmegaConf when hya is imported, so register_resolvers() does not replace them silently: it skips the key and emits a warning. Use replace=True to replace the resolver of OmegaConf:

from hya import get_default_registry

registry = get_default_registry()


@registry.register("hya.add", exist_ok=True)
def custom_add(first, *others):
    """Custom add that also prints the result."""
    result = first
    for other in others:
        result = result + other
    print(f"Adding {(first, *others)} = {result}")
    return result


# Without replace=True, the published resolver is kept and a warning is emitted.
# With replace=True, the resolver of OmegaConf is replaced by custom_add.
registry.register_resolvers(replace=True)

register_resolvers is idempotent: calling it twice changes nothing. A resolver removed from OmegaConf (for example by OmegaConf.clear_resolvers()) is published again. A key that another source registered in OmegaConf is not overwritten unless replace=True: one warning lists the skipped keys, after the other keys are published. With replace=True, every key of the registry is published, whatever OmegaConf holds. A resolver that another source registers over a key that the registry already published is kept without a warning: use replace=True to publish yours again.

OmegaConf caches the value of the nodes it has already resolved. Replacing a resolver does not clear this cache for existing configurations: call OmegaConf.clear_cache(cfg) to clear it.

With OmegaConf 2.4 and later, the resolvers are published with annotation_validation="off": the type annotations of a resolver are documentation for readers and type checkers, OmegaConf does not check them at call time.

docs.title: Registering a Resolver Lazily
docs.text:
register_lazy registers a resolver as a "module:function" string. The module is imported the first time OmegaConf calls the resolver, not when the resolver is registered. This is how hya registers the resolvers that need a heavy optional package:

from hya import get_default_registry

registry = get_default_registry()
# "statistics" is imported when ${my.mean:...} is called for the first time
registry.register_lazy("my.mean", "statistics:mean")
registry.register_resolvers()

average: ${my.mean:[1,2,6]} # 3

A target that is not formatted as "module:function", with an absolute module name made of names joined by dots and a function name that is a Python identifier, raises a ValueError when it is registered, and a target that is not a string raises a TypeError. An unknown module or function raises an error on the first call of the resolver. A lazy resolver cannot receive the special parameters of OmegaConf (_root_, _parent_, _node_): register such a resolver with register.

docs.title: Creating Isolated Registries
docs.text:
For advanced use cases, you can create independent registries:

from hya.registry import ResolverRegistry

# Create a new, isolated registry
custom_registry = ResolverRegistry()


@custom_registry.register("custom.multiply")
def multiply(x, y):
    return x * y


# Register only these custom resolvers
custom_registry.register_resolvers()

ResolverRegistry is also available from the top-level package: from hya import ResolverRegistry. Its constructor takes an optional mapping of keys to resolvers, validated as by register; anything else than a mapping or None raises a TypeError.

docs.title: Reading Configuration Values
docs.text:
A resolver receives a list or a mapping of the configuration as a configuration node (ListConfig or DictConfig), and a literal such as [${x}] as a list that holds nodes. If your resolver reads a whole value as data, convert it first with hya.utils.config.to_plain: it resolves the interpolations at any depth, raises on a missing value (???), and returns plain lists and dictionaries without modifying the configuration.

import hya
from hya import get_default_registry
from hya.utils.config import to_plain
from omegaconf import OmegaConf

registry = get_default_registry()


@registry.register("my.unique")
def unique_resolver(values):
    return list(dict.fromkeys(to_plain(values)))


registry.register_resolvers()

conf = OmegaConf.create({"a": "x", "names": ["${a}", "y", "x"], "unique": "${my.unique:${names}}"})
print(conf.unique)  # Output: ['x', 'y']

docs.title: Reading Other Keys
docs.text:
OmegaConf gives a resolver the special keyword arguments _root_ (the whole configuration) and _parent_ (the node that holds the interpolation) when its signature declares them:

from hya import get_default_registry
from omegaconf import OmegaConf

registry = get_default_registry()


@registry.register("my.sibling")
def sibling_resolver(key, *, _parent_):
    return _parent_[key]


registry.register_resolvers()

conf = OmegaConf.create({"model": {"size": 4, "alias": "${my.sibling:size}"}})
print(conf.model.alias)  # Output: 4

docs.title: Optional Dependencies in a Resolver
docs.text:
hya.imports checks the packages that hya knows (braceexpand, numpy and torch): is_<package>_available returns a boolean without importing the package, and validate_<package> raises a RuntimeError that says how to install it.

from hya import get_default_registry
from hya.imports import validate_numpy

registry = get_default_registry()


@registry.register("my.zeros")
def zeros_resolver(size):
    validate_numpy()
    import numpy as np

    return np.zeros(size)


registry.register_resolvers()

docs.title: Testing with Optional Dependencies
docs.text:
hya.testing provides pytest marks that skip a test depending on the installed packages. Install it with the testing extra (pip install 'hya[testing]').

Mark The test runs when braceexpand_available braceexpand is installed braceexpand_not_available braceexpand is not installed numpy_available numpy is installed numpy_not_available numpy is not installed torch_available torch is installed torch_not_available torch is not installed 
import hya
from hya.testing import numpy_available
from omegaconf import OmegaConf


@numpy_available
def test_array() -> None:
    conf = OmegaConf.create({"x": "${hya.np.array:[1,2]}"})
    assert conf.x.tolist() == [1, 2]

docs.title: Checking for Resolvers
docs.text:
Check if a resolver is registered:

from hya import get_default_registry

registry = get_default_registry()

# Check if a resolver exists
if registry.has_resolver("hya.add"):
    print("add resolver is available")

# List all registered resolvers
for key in registry.state.keys():
    print(f"Registered: {key}")

docs.title: Accessing Registry State
docs.text:
from hya import get_default_registry

registry = get_default_registry()

# Get all registered resolvers: a read-only mapping (use registry.register to add one)
resolvers_dict = registry.state

# Count resolvers
print(f"Total resolvers: {len(resolvers_dict)}")

# Check specific resolvers
core_resolvers = [k for k in resolvers_dict.keys() if k.startswith("hya.")]
print(f"Core hya resolvers: {len(core_resolvers)}")

docs.title: Design Choices
docs.text: This page explains how hya is designed and why. Each choice has a cost, so each section states the trade-off and what to do when the choice does not fit your project. The rules that follow from these choices are listed in Properties.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
hya has three parts:

Part Module Role Resolvers hya.resolvers, hya.numpy, hya.torch, hya.braceexpand The functions that a configuration calls Registry hya.registry Maps keys to resolvers and publishes them Default registry hya.default The keys of hya, published when hya is imported

A value goes through them as follows:

  1. import hya publishes the default registry to the resolver table of OmegaConf.
  2. A configuration holds an interpolation, such as ${hya.add:${x},1}. Loading the configuration does not call any resolver.
  3. When the value is accessed, OmegaConf resolves the references of the arguments and calls the resolver, which imports its optional package if it has one.
  4. The output is returned to your code. OmegaConf does not keep it: the next access calls the resolver again.

hya uses the public API of OmegaConf only. The modules that need an optional package are independent of each other, and the default registry does not import them.

docs.title: Resolvers are standard library callables when possible
docs.text:
hya.sub, hya.sqrt, hya.max, hya.len, hya.int, ... are registered as the callable itself (operator.sub, math.sqrt, max, len, int), with no wrapper.

  • Benefit: the behaviour, the accepted arguments and the error messages are the ones of the standard library, which you already know and which are documented. There is no hya code to read or to trust.
  • Cost: hya cannot smooth the rough edges of a callable. hya.max takes the arguments of max (${hya.max:10,25,15}), and hya.log raises the ValueError of math.log for a value outside its domain.
  • If it does not fit: register your own resolver (see Custom Resolvers).

A resolver is a function of a few lines only when no standard library callable has the behaviour (hya.add, hya.mul, hya.ceildiv, hya.path, hya.iter_join, hya.sha256, hya.pi).

docs.title: The set of resolvers is small
docs.text:
hya has one resolver for one operation that a configuration needs, not a copy of the standard library. For example, there is no hya.abs, hya.round or hya.mod, and there is no bool or str cast (bool("false") is True, and an interpolation already produces a string).

  • Benefit: the whole library fits in one page and each key has one meaning.
  • Cost: an operation that is missing needs a custom resolver (two lines, see Custom Resolvers).

docs.title: Optional resolvers are always registered, and imported lazily
docs.text:
hya.braceexpand, hya.np.array, hya.torch.tensor and hya.torch.dtype are in the registry on every machine. Their module, and so numpy, torch or braceexpand, is imported when OmegaConf calls the resolver for the first time (ResolverRegistry.register_lazy).

  • Benefit: import hya is fast and does not import numpy, torch or braceexpand. The registry has the same keys everywhere, so a configuration that is valid on one machine fails with the same error on another machine that lacks the package.
  • Cost: a missing package is detected when the resolver is called, not when hya is imported or when the configuration is loaded.
  • If it does not fit: call the resolver once at start up, or check the package with hya.imports before you load the configuration.

A lazy resolver cannot receive the special parameters of OmegaConf (_root_, _parent_, _node_): OmegaConf reads them from the signature of the function, which is not known before the import. Register such a resolver with register.

A missing package raises a RuntimeError that says how to install it ('torch' package is required but not installed. ... pip install torch).

docs.title: Every key lives in the hya. namespace
docs.text:
Built-in keys start with hya., and optional ones are grouped by package (hya.np.*, hya.torch.*).

  • Benefit: hya never collides with the resolvers of OmegaConf (oc.*), of Hydra (hydra) or of your project.
  • Cost: the keys are longer than add or mul.
  • If it does not fit: register an alias in your own registry, for example my.add.

docs.title: Importing hya registers the resolvers
docs.text:
import hya publishes the default resolvers to OmegaConf. No other call is needed.

  • Benefit: the common case is one line, in a script or in a Hydra application.
  • Cost: importing a package has a side effect on a global (the resolver table of OmegaConf). The import must happen before the configuration is resolved, so a module that only loads a YAML file still needs import hya.
  • If it does not fit: build a ResolverRegistry of your own and call register_resolvers() when you decide to. Importing hya still publishes the default resolvers.

Hydra has a plugin mechanism that could remove the import. hya does not use it: it needs a hydra_plugins namespace package and a dependency on Hydra internals for the gain of one line.

docs.title: The registry rejects what cannot work
docs.text:
Every entry of a ResolverRegistry is added by register, including the ones of the constructor and of register_lazy. It raises at once for a value that is not callable, a key that is not a string (@registry.register used without a key) and a key that is not made of names joined by dots. The constructor raises for anything else than a mapping or None, and register_lazy for a target that is not a string formatted as module:function, made of names.

  • Benefit: the error points at the line that registers, not at a configuration that fails to parse later, and register_resolvers() cannot stop half way because of an entry.
  • Cost: a key such as my-key, which OmegaConf 2.3 and later can interpolate, is rejected, because OmegaConf 2.2 cannot interpolate it and hya behaves the same on all of them.
  • If it does not fit: register such a resolver with OmegaConf directly.

docs.title: The registry is explicit about replacing
docs.text:
A ResolverRegistry is a map from a key to a callable, with two separate steps: register adds a callable to the registry, and register_resolvers publishes the registry to OmegaConf. Both refuse to replace silently:

  • register(key) raises a RuntimeError if the key exists, unless exist_ok=True.

  • register_resolvers() skips a key that OmegaConf already has and that the registry did not publish, unless replace=True. One warning lists the skipped keys, after the other keys are published. With replace=True, every key is published, whatever OmegaConf holds.

  • Benefit: a typo or an import-order accident cannot swap a resolver without a trace, and register_resolvers() can be called as often as you like (it is idempotent).

  • Cost: overriding a built-in takes two opt-ins (exist_ok=True, then replace=True).
  • Limit: hya cannot detect that another source registered a key in OmegaConf after hya published it: register_resolvers() keeps it silently. Doing so needs private OmegaConf attributes that change between releases. Use replace=True to publish the key again.

docs.title: Errors are the ones of OmegaConf
docs.text:
A resolver raises standard exceptions only, and OmegaConf reports a failure as an InterpolationResolutionError. hya does not wrap the error in an exception of its own, and no resolver raises an OmegaConf error of its own accord: a direct Python call of torch_dtype_resolver raises a plain ValueError.

  • Benefit: there is no extra layer between you and the real error. The message names the original exception, which is in the __context__ chain of the error (__cause__ is None).
  • Cost: you cannot catch "any hya error" with one except clause; you catch the OmegaConf error and inspect its context.

docs.title: The resolvers of hya follow one contract
docs.text:
A standard library resolver is the callable itself, with its behaviour. A resolver written by hya follows four rules:

  1. Read resolved input. An argument that is a list or a mapping goes through hya.utils.config.to_plain before it is used, so no resolver computes on a configuration node. hya.mul and hya.ceildiv take numbers and hya.path takes one path, so the rule does not apply to them.
  2. Return a new list, dictionary, array or tensor.
  3. Raise rather than guess or drop a part of the input.

  4. Keep no state.

  5. Benefit: a resolver gives the same result for a literal and for a reference, works with a read-only configuration, and its result can be mutated without changing the configuration.

  6. Cost: resolving a large list at each access takes time, and a list returned by hya.add no longer holds interpolations or the API of a configuration node.
  7. If it does not fit: use ${x} to get the node x itself, or register your own resolver.

docs.title: Resolvers are pure and can return any object
docs.text:
A resolver never modifies its arguments: ${hya.add:${x},[3]} returns a new list and leaves x unchanged, and ${hya.add:${x}} is a copy of x. A standard library callable can return an argument or one of its elements (hya.max of several values), as ${x} returns the node x, so copy such a value before you mutate it. A resolver may return any Python object (Path, ndarray, Tensor, dtype, list).

  • Benefit: a configuration can carry the objects your code needs, with no conversion step.
  • Cost: an array, a tensor or a data type is not a value of a configuration. Use it in code, or with OmegaConf.to_container(cfg, resolve=True). OmegaConf.resolve needs the allow_objects flag for it, and OmegaConf.to_yaml with resolve=True does not support it.

docs.title: Arguments are positional
docs.text:
The arguments of a resolver are positional, because the interpolation grammar has no keyword syntax. An optional argument comes last and has a default (${hya.np.array:[1,2],float32}). The options of the Python API (exist_ok, replace) are keyword-only.

  • Benefit: the YAML and the Python API each use the form that is natural to them, and an option cannot be swapped with another by position.
  • Cost: a resolver with many options would be hard to read; hya keeps resolvers to a few arguments.

docs.title: Annotations are documentation, not validation
docs.text:
With OmegaConf 2.4 and later, hya publishes resolvers with annotation_validation="off". The type annotations describe the resolver for readers and type checkers; OmegaConf does not check them at call time.

  • Benefit: the same resolver behaves the same on every supported OmegaConf release (2.2 to 2.4), and a resolver that accepts several types is not rejected by an annotation.
  • Cost: a wrong type fails inside the resolver (for example a TypeError) instead of in a validation step.

docs.title: The hash reads the whole value
docs.text:
hya.sha256 is meant for identifiers, so two different values must not share a hash by accident. It resolves the configuration nodes of its argument (hya.utils.config.to_plain, the first rule of the contract), then hashes a string as is and any other value as canonical JSON (sorted keys, no space, non-ASCII characters escaped).

  • Benefit: the hash follows the interpolated values, does not depend on the order of the keys, on repr, on the print options of NumPy or PyTorch, or on the OmegaConf release, and the hash of a string is the one that other SHA-256 tools give.
  • Cost: the type of a value is not part of the hash (the string [1] and the list [1] have the same hash), a value without a JSON form raises instead of being hashed, and resolving a large list at each access takes time.
  • If it does not fit: hash the value in your code, or register your own resolver.

An array or a tensor is not hashed from its bytes: it would need a format for the data type and the shape, and two optional packages in a resolver of the standard library. Hash the value the array is built from.

docs.title: Some behaviours follow Python on purpose
docs.text:
• hya.ceildiv follows //. It computes -(a // -b), which is exact for integers of any size. The result is an int for two integers and a float for a float. Use ${hya.int:${hya.ceildiv:x,y}} to force an int.
  • hya.torch.dtype accepts names, not torch.float32. There is one spelling for one thing, and the error for an unknown name lists the valid names, sorted. hya.torch.tensor accepts the same names.
  • hya.np.array takes the data type as a string. The string that NumPy accepts is enough, so there is no hya.np.dtype resolver. hya.torch.tensor takes the name too, so the two resolvers have the same contract, and also a torch.dtype, such as the output of hya.torch.dtype.
  • hya.path reads file: URLs only. A string that starts with file: is decoded as a URL. A file URL with a host other than localhost, a query or a fragment raises a ValueError instead of dropping it: write a ? or a # of a file name as %3F or %23. Any other scheme:// string and an empty path raise too, because the path they would give is not what the configuration means, and the failure would appear far from its cause. Any other string is a plain path, so /data/a%20b keeps its %20.
  • hya.braceexpand returns a list. It has a length, can be indexed and can be read several times, at the cost of building the whole expansion at once.

docs.title: Compatibility with Hydra
docs.text: hya accepts every OmegaConf release that Hydra 1.3 accepts (omegaconf>=2.2,<3.0), so it can be installed next to any hydra-core 1.3 release. The only code that depends on the OmegaConf version is the function that publishes a resolver (register_resolver in 2.4 and later, register_new_resolver before).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.11 or later.
  • omegaconf>=2.2,<3.0, installed with hya.

It is highly recommended to install in a virtual environment to keep your system in order.

docs.title: Installing with uv (recommended)
docs.text:
The following command installs the latest release of the library:

uv pip install hya

docs.title: Installing with pip
docs.text:
pip install hya

To make the package as slim as possible, only the packages required to use hya are installed. This minimal installation includes only omegaconf, which is sufficient for using all the core resolvers.

docs.title: Installing Optional Dependencies
docs.text:
hya provides additional resolvers that require optional dependencies. Each one has an extra, which installs a supported version of the package:

uv pip install 'hya[braceexpand]' # For the hya.braceexpand resolver
uv pip install 'hya[numpy]'       # For the hya.np.array resolver
uv pip install 'hya[torch]'       # For the hya.torch.tensor and hya.torch.dtype resolvers
uv pip install 'hya[testing]'     # For the pytest marks of hya.testing

# Install all optional dependencies, including pytest (the testing extra)
uv pip install 'hya[all]'

The quotes are needed by some shells, such as zsh. Several extras can be combined, for example 'hya[numpy,torch]'.

The torch extra installs PyTorch on Linux and on macOS with Apple Silicon only. On another platform it installs nothing: follow the PyTorch installation instructions.

docs.title: Dependency Matrix
docs.text:
The following table shows which features require which packages:

Feature Required Package Description hya.braceexpand braceexpand>=0.1.7,<0.2 Brace expansion patterns hya.np.array numpy>=2.0,<3.0 NumPy array creation hya.torch.tensor torch>=2.4,<3.0 PyTorch tensor creation hya.torch.dtype torch>=2.4,<3.0 PyTorch data type specification hya.testing pytest>=9.0,<10.0 Pytest marks

All other resolvers work with the base installation (only omegaconf required).

The optional resolvers are registered even when their package is missing. Calling one of them then raises an error that says which package to install, for example 'torch' package is required but not installed. ... pip install torch.

docs.title: Checking the installation
docs.text:
The following script prints the version of hya and resolves a configuration:

import hya
from omegaconf import OmegaConf

print(hya.__version__)
conf = OmegaConf.create({"result": "${hya.add:1,2}"})
print(conf.result)  # Output: 3

The next step is the User Guide.

docs.title: Installing from source
docs.text:
To install hya from source, you can follow the steps below. First, you will need to install uv. uv is used to manage and install the dependencies. If uv is already installed on your machine, you can skip this step. You can check the uv installation by running the following command:

uv --version

Then, you can clone the git repository:

git clone git@github.com:durandtibo/hya.git

Then, create the virtual environment and install hya with the following commands:

cd hya
make setup-venv
source .venv/bin/activate

make setup-venv installs uv if it is missing and updates it, creates a Python 3.14 virtual environment in .venv (it replaces an existing one), and installs hya in editable mode with all its dependencies. It asks you to confirm that .venv can be cleared: answer y, as any other answer stops the installation.

Once the virtual environment is activated, you can install the dependencies again with the following command:

inv env.install

You can also use this command to restore the environment to the versions of the lock file (uv.lock). To update the dependencies to more recent versions, use inv env.update.

Finally, you can test the installation with the following commands:

inv test.unit --cov
inv test.integration

Run inv --list to see all the tasks.

docs.title: Using with Hydra
docs.text:
hya is designed to be used with Hydra. Hydra is not a dependency of hya: install it with pip install hydra-core.

Add import hya to the module of your application. It registers the resolvers before Hydra resolves the configuration.

Python 3.14: with hydra-core 1.3.8, an application decorated with @hydra.main stops with ValueError: badly formed help string before your code runs. The error comes from Hydra, not from hya. Use Python 3.11 to 3.13 with this Hydra release.

docs.title: Basic Example
docs.text:
config.yaml:

dataset:
  name: mnist
  train_samples: 60000
  val_samples: 10000
  total_samples: ${hya.add:${dataset.train_samples},${dataset.val_samples}}

model:
  type: cnn
  channels: [32, 64, 128]
  num_layers: ${hya.len:${model.channels}}

training:
  batch_size: 64
  epochs: 10
  steps_per_epoch: ${hya.ceildiv:${dataset.train_samples},${training.batch_size}}

paths:
  root: /data
  train: ${hya.iter_join:[${paths.root},${dataset.name},train],/}
  val: ${hya.iter_join:[${paths.root},${dataset.name},val],/}

experiment:
  name: ${dataset.name}_${model.type}
  version: ${hya.sha256:${experiment.name}}

train.py:

import hya
import hydra
from omegaconf import DictConfig


@hydra.main(version_base=None, config_path=".", config_name="config")
def train(cfg: DictConfig):
    print(f"Dataset: {cfg.dataset.name}")
    print(f"Total samples: {cfg.dataset.total_samples}")
    print(f"Model layers: {cfg.model.num_layers}")
    print(f"Steps per epoch: {cfg.training.steps_per_epoch}")
    print(f"Train path: {cfg.paths.train}")
    print(f"Experiment version: {cfg.experiment.version}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    train()

docs.title: Multiple Configuration Files
docs.text:
You can use hya resolvers across multiple configuration files. The files of the groups are in the model/ and optimizer/ directories, next to config.yaml, and each one is composed under the name of its directory, so a reference starts with that name (${model.depth}):

config.yaml:

defaults:
  - model: resnet
  - optimizer: adam
  - _self_

experiment:
  name: ${model.name}_${optimizer.name}
  seed: 42
  version: ${hya.sha256:${experiment.name}_${experiment.seed}}

model/resnet.yaml:

name: resnet
depth: 50
width_multiplier: 1.0
effective_depth: ${hya.mul:${model.depth},${model.width_multiplier}}

optimizer/adam.yaml:

name: adam
lr: ${hya.pow:10,-4} # 0.0001
betas: [0.9, 0.999]

docs.title: Command Line Overrides
docs.text:
The values that a resolver reads can be overridden, and the computed values follow. With the configuration of the previous section:

python train.py model.depth=101

An override can call a resolver. Quote it, so the shell does not read $ and the braces:

python train.py 'experiment.seed=${hya.add:40,3}'

A multi-run resolves the resolvers in each job:

python train.py -m model.depth=18,34

docs.title: Output Directory
docs.text:
The configuration of Hydra can use the resolvers too, for example to name the output directory after a hash. Add to config.yaml:

hydra:
  run:
    dir: outputs/${hya.sha256:${experiment.name}}

docs.title: Resolving the Whole Configuration
docs.text:
Hydra gives your function a configuration with unresolved interpolations. To fail early, for example before a long training, resolve a copy at the start of the application:

from omegaconf import DictConfig, OmegaConf


def check_config(cfg: DictConfig) -> None:
    # Raises if an interpolation cannot be resolved or if a value is missing (???)
    OmegaConf.to_container(cfg, resolve=True, throw_on_missing=True)

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
These are the rules hya guarantees. The Design Choices page explains the reasons and the trade-offs, and the limits list what hya does not guarantee. Each rule has a number, so that other pages can refer to it.

Group Properties Import and registry P1 Import is enough, P2 Cheap import, P3 Namespaced, P7 Explicit, strict registry, P8 Replace is explicit, P9 One default registry Behaviour of the resolvers P4 Thin resolvers, P5 Pure, P6 Deterministic output, P16 Resolved input, P17 Faithful hash, P15 Composable Values and errors P10 Errors are OmegaConf's, P11 Any value out Python API and compatibility P13 Keyword-only options, P12 Typed and documented, P14 Installs next to Hydra

docs.title: P1: Import is enough
docs.text: import hya registers every available default resolver with OmegaConf. No other call is needed, and register_resolvers() publishes them again after OmegaConf.clear_resolvers().

docs.title: P2: Cheap import
docs.text:
import hya imports neither numpy, torch nor braceexpand, and emits no warning when no other source has registered a hya. key. The module of an optional resolver is imported on the first call of that resolver.

The optional resolvers are registered with ResolverRegistry.register_lazy, and import hya does not look for their packages on disk.

docs.title: P3: Namespaced
docs.text: Every built-in key starts with hya.. Optional ones are grouped (hya.np.*, hya.torch.*). Nothing is registered outside this namespace.

docs.title: P7: Explicit, strict registry
docs.text:
A ResolverRegistry is a key to callable map. register adds, register_resolvers publishes. The constructor takes a mapping or None. Every entry has a callable value and a key that every supported OmegaConf can interpolate, and every lazy target is module:function made of names; anything else raises at registration.

A key is made of names joined by dots, where a name is made of ASCII letters, digits and _ and does not start with a digit. OmegaConf 2.3 and later can interpolate a - too, but OmegaConf 2.2 cannot, so hya rejects it (P14). The module of a lazy target follows the rule of the keys (so it cannot be relative, as .numpy) and its function is a Python identifier. That they exist is checked on the first call. A registry is independent of the other registries.

docs.title: P8: Replace is explicit
docs.text:
register_resolvers() is idempotent. A key that changed since it was published, or that another source registered before the registry published it, is skipped unless replace=True; one warning lists the skipped keys, after the other keys are published. With replace=True, every key of the registry is published, whatever OmegaConf holds.

After import hya, the default resolvers are already published, so registry.register_resolvers() is silent. Overriding a built-in (registry.register("hya.add", exist_ok=True)) warns until register_resolvers(replace=True) is called. OmegaConf caches the resolved nodes of a configuration: replace=True does not clear the cache of the existing configurations (OmegaConf.clear_cache(cfg)).

docs.title: P9: One default registry
docs.text: get_default_registry() returns one process-wide registry holding the built-in resolvers. It holds the same keys on every machine, whatever packages are installed. Users extend it or create their own registry.

docs.title: P4: Thin resolvers
docs.text: A resolver is a standard library callable or a function of a few lines with one documented behaviour. No hidden state, no I/O beyond what its name says (hya.path touches the file system). A resolver written by hya raises on an input it cannot honour instead of guessing or dropping a part of it.

docs.title: P5: Pure
docs.text: A resolver never modifies its arguments. A resolver written by hya returns a new list, dictionary or array and never a container of an argument; hya.torch.tensor returns a copy (hya.add of a single other object returns it, and so does hya.mul, which takes numbers, of its single argument). A standard library callable can return an argument or one of its elements (hya.max of several values), as ${x} returns the node x: copy it before you mutate it.

docs.title: P6: Deterministic output
docs.text: The same resolved arguments give the same output, including error messages (sorted, no set order), on every process and OmegaConf release. The type of the result of a resolver written by hya does not depend on how an argument is written (a literal or a reference), as long as it takes the argument (hya.mul takes numbers). hya.path also depends on the file system (working directory, home directory, symbolic links), which is its purpose.

docs.title: P16: Resolved input
docs.text: A resolver written by hya that reads a list or a mapping (hya.add, hya.sha256, hya.iter_join, hya.np.array, hya.torch.tensor) reads its resolved content: interpolations are resolved at any depth, and a missing value (???) raises MissingMandatoryValue.

docs.title: P17: Faithful hash
docs.text: hya.sha256 hashes the whole content of a value: a string as is, any other value as canonical JSON (sorted keys, no space, non-ASCII escaped). Two such values with different JSON forms have different hashes, and a value without a JSON form (a non-finite float included) raises.

docs.title: P15: Composable
docs.text: A resolver written by hya accepts the values OmegaConf gives it (str, int, float, bool, None, list, dict, ListConfig, DictConfig), from a writable or a read-only configuration, and the output of another hya resolver of a type it takes (a Path for hya.path, a torch.dtype for hya.torch.tensor), without a warning. hya.np.array and hya.torch.tensor take a tensor (on the CPU, without gradient for NumPy) and an array, and hya.torch.tensor takes a data type as a torch.dtype or as its name.

docs.title: P10: Errors are OmegaConf's
docs.text:
A resolver raises standard exceptions only, so a failure surfaces as InterpolationResolutionError whose message names the original exception, found in the __context__ chain (__cause__ is None). A missing optional package says how to install it.

A missing configuration value (???) is reported by the exceptions of OmegaConf (MissingMandatoryValue, which the message names). hya adds no exception class of its own and no wrapper. With OmegaConf 2.4 and later, the annotations of the resolvers published by hya are not validated at call time.

docs.title: P11: Any value out
docs.text:
A resolver may return any Python object (Path, ndarray, Tensor, dtype, list). Such values are for use in code: for an array, a tensor or a data type, OmegaConf.resolve needs the allow_objects flag and to_yaml does not support them.

Use such a value in code (cfg.key, or OmegaConf.to_container(cfg, resolve=True)). To resolve a whole configuration in place, give it the allow_objects flag, when you create it (OmegaConf.create(..., flags={"allow_objects": True})) or around the call (with flag_override(cfg, "allow_objects", True): OmegaConf.resolve(cfg), with from omegaconf import flag_override).

docs.title: P13: Keyword-only options
docs.text: The options of the Python API are keyword-only (exist_ok, replace). The arguments of a resolver are positional, because the interpolation grammar has no keyword syntax; an optional argument of a resolver comes last and has a default.

docs.title: P12: Typed and documented
docs.text: The package has a py.typed file and its public types are complete (pyright --verifytypes scores 100 %). Every public function, class, method and property has a docstring with an example and is shown in the reference, and every default key is listed in the resolvers page.

docs.title: P14: Installs next to Hydra
docs.text: hya accepts every OmegaConf release that a Hydra release accepts (omegaconf>=2.2,<3.0) and behaves the same on all of them. CI runs the tests on the oldest and the newest.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
hya does not provide the following.

  • Thread-safety of registering resolvers while OmegaConf resolves interpolations. The resolver table of OmegaConf is a global dictionary.
  • Detection of a conflicting registration. register_resolvers() without replace=True keeps silently a resolver that another source registered over a published key: detecting it needs the private BaseContainer._resolvers of OmegaConf, which changes between releases. register_resolvers(replace=True) publishes the key again.
  • Type-tagged hashes. hya.sha256 of the string [1] equals the hash of the list [1], an integer key equals the same string key, a path or an enum equals its string in JSON, and an enum that is also an int, a float or a str equals its value. A mapping that mixes key types cannot be sorted and raises.
  • Special parameters of lazy resolvers. A resolver registered with register_lazy cannot receive _root_, _parent_ or _node_: OmegaConf reads them from the signature, which is not known before the import.
  • Warnings of the libraries for inputs they discourage, for example torch.tensor of a list of NumPy arrays.
  • Caching of the output of the resolvers. OmegaConf does not cache it: every access of an interpolation calls the resolver again.
  • Export of objects. OmegaConf.to_yaml(resolve=True) does not support an array, a tensor or a data type, and OmegaConf.resolve needs the allow_objects flag for them (P11).

docs.title: Resolvers
docs.text: This page provides comprehensive documentation for all resolvers implemented in hya.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
hya provides 24 built-in resolvers and 4 optional resolvers for use in OmegaConf/Hydra configurations. All keys start with hya.:

Category Resolvers Arithmetic add, sub, mul, truediv, floordiv, ceildiv, neg Math Functions pow, sqrt, exp, log, log10, sinh, asinh Comparison max, min Casts int, float Collections len, sum Constants pi Paths path, iter_join Hashing sha256 Optional braceexpand, np.array, torch.tensor, torch.dtype

There are two kinds of resolvers:

  • Standard library resolvers are the callable itself, with its own behaviour and errors.
  • The other resolvers are written by hya. They are documented one by one below.

All resolvers are available after importing hya. The optional resolvers are registered too; the package they need is imported when they are called. See Interpolation Syntax for the rules to write the arguments.

An error raised by a resolver is reported by OmegaConf as an InterpolationResolutionError whose message names the original error. The errors listed below are the original ones.

docs.title: Default Resolvers
docs.text: These resolvers are available with the base installation (no optional dependencies required).

docs.title: Standard Library Resolvers
docs.text:
These resolvers are registered as the standard library callable itself, with no wrapper: the behaviour, the accepted arguments and the error messages are the ones of the callable. See the documentation of the callable for the details.

Key Callable Example Result hya.sub operator.sub ${hya.sub:100,30} 70 hya.truediv operator.truediv ${hya.truediv:10,4} 2.5 hya.floordiv operator.floordiv ${hya.floordiv:100,32} 3 hya.neg operator.neg ${hya.neg:5} -5 hya.pow operator.pow ${hya.pow:10,-3} 0.001 hya.sqrt math.sqrt ${hya.sqrt:64} 8.0 hya.exp math.exp ${hya.exp:0} 1.0 hya.log math.log ${hya.log:8,2} 3.0 hya.log10 math.log10 ${hya.log10:1000} 3.0 hya.sinh math.sinh ${hya.sinh:0} 0.0 hya.asinh math.asinh ${hya.asinh:0} 0.0 hya.max max ${hya.max:10,25,15} 25 hya.min min ${hya.min:10,25,15} 10 hya.len len ${hya.len:[1,2,3]} 3 hya.sum sum ${hya.sum:[1,2,3]} 6 hya.int int ${hya.int:${hya.mul:100000,0.1}} 10000 hya.float float ${hya.float:3} 3.0

Examples with interpolations:

dataset:
  total_samples: 60000
  val_samples: 10000
  train_samples: ${hya.sub:${dataset.total_samples},${dataset.val_samples}} # 50000
  warmup_ratio: ${hya.truediv:1000,${dataset.total_samples}} # 0.016666...

model:
  embedding_dim: 512
  head_dim: ${hya.floordiv:${model.embedding_dim},8} # 64
  scale_factor: ${hya.sqrt:${model.embedding_dim}} # 22.627...
  layer_sizes: [128, 256, 512, 1024]
  num_layers: ${hya.len:${model.layer_sizes}} # 4
  actual_layers: ${hya.max:${model.num_layers},8} # 8
  total_units: ${hya.sum:${model.layer_sizes}} # 1920

hya.int casts the float of a computation back to an integer, and hya.sum adds the elements of a list (hya.add takes values: ${hya.add:${model.layer_sizes}} returns a copy of the list). bool and str have no resolver: bool("false") is True, and str is what an interpolation already does. See Design Choices for why these resolvers have no wrapper.

docs.title: hya.add
docs.text:
Adds multiple values together.

Syntax: ${hya.add:value1,value2,...}

Example:

# Simple addition
total: ${hya.add:10,20} # Result: 30

# Multiple values
sum: ${hya.add:1,2,3,4,5} # Result: 15

# With references
training:
  train_samples: 50000
  val_samples: 10000
  total_samples: ${hya.add:${training.train_samples},${training.val_samples}} # Result: 60000

Equivalent Python:

# the values are the resolved content of the arguments, without configuration nodes
value = value1 + value2 + value3 + ...

Notes:

  • The arguments are never modified: ${hya.add:${x},[3]} returns a new list and leaves x unchanged. ${hya.add:${x}} returns a copy of x.
  • Adding lists gives a plain list, whether they are written in the interpolation or referenced (${x}). It also works with a read-only configuration.
  • The interpolations of the values are resolved at any depth, and a missing value (???) is an error. The result holds the resolved values, no interpolation.
  • At least one argument is required.
  • Values that cannot be added, such as a number and a string, raise a TypeError.

docs.title: hya.mul
docs.text:
Multiplies multiple values together.

Syntax: ${hya.mul:value1,value2,...}

Example:

# Simple multiplication
area: ${hya.mul:10,20} # Result: 200

# Multiple values
volume: ${hya.mul:5,10,2} # Result: 100

# Compute total parameters
model:
  layers: 12
  hidden_size: 768
  total_params: ${hya.mul:${model.layers},${model.hidden_size}} # Result: 9216

Equivalent Python:

value = object1 * object2 * object3 * ...

Notes:

  • The arguments are never modified and are meant to be numbers. Repeating a list of the configuration (${hya.mul:${x},2} with x: [1, 2]) is not supported and raises a TypeError: repeat the list in your code.
  • At least one argument is required.

docs.title: hya.ceildiv
docs.text:
Performs ceiling division (rounds up). The type of the result follows //: an int for two integers (exact, whatever their size) and a float for a float (${hya.ceildiv:11.0,4} is 3.0). Use ${hya.int:${hya.ceildiv:x,y}} to get an int.

Syntax: ${hya.ceildiv:dividend,divisor}

Example:

batches: ${hya.ceildiv:100,32} # Result: 4

# Calculate number of batches needed
training:
  samples: 10000
  batch_size: 64
  num_batches: ${hya.ceildiv:${training.samples},${training.batch_size}} # Result: 157

Equivalent Python:

value = -(dividend // -divisor)  # Canonical implementation (no floating point)
# math.ceil(dividend / divisor) gives the same integer for small ints, but it may have
# precision issues with large integers and it always returns an int

Errors: ZeroDivisionError for a divisor of zero, and TypeError for a value that is not a number.

Use Case: Calculating the number of batches needed to process all samples.

docs.title: hya.pi
docs.text:
Returns the mathematical constant π (pi).

Syntax: ${hya.pi:}

Example:

pi_value: ${hya.pi:} # Result: 3.14159...

geometry:
  radius: 5
  circumference: ${hya.mul:2,${hya.pi:},${geometry.radius}} # Result: 31.41...

Equivalent Python:

import math

value = math.pi

docs.title: hya.path
docs.text:
Converts a string, a path-like object, or a file: URL, to a resolved pathlib.Path object with user expansion.

Syntax: ${hya.path:path_string}

Example:

data_dir: ${hya.path:/data/datasets}
model_path: ${hya.path:"~/models/checkpoint.pth"}
local_file: ${hya.path:file:///data/file.txt}
url_decoded: ${hya.path:file:///data/my%20file.txt} # /data/my file.txt

Equivalent Python:

import os
import re
from pathlib import Path
from urllib.parse import unquote, urlparse

path = os.fspath(path)
if not path:
    raise ValueError("The path is empty")
url = urlparse(path)
if url.scheme == "file":
    if url.netloc.lower() not in ("", "localhost") or "?" in path or "#" in path:
        raise ValueError(
            f"A file URL with a host, a query or a fragment is not supported: '{path}'"
        )
    if not url.path:
        raise ValueError(f"The file URL has no path: '{path}'")
    path = unquote(url.path, errors="strict")
elif re.match(r"\s*[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9+.-]+://", path):
    raise ValueError(f"Only a file URL can be converted to a path, but received '{path}'")
value = Path(path).expanduser().resolve()

Notes:

  • Returns a pathlib.Path object, which is useful for path operations in Python.
  • An empty path raises a ValueError, so an empty value does not point at the working directory: write . for it.
  • Only a string that starts with file: (the scheme is case-insensitive) is read as a URL (its percent-encoding is decoded). A host other than localhost (file://host/a, the host name is case-insensitive), a query or a fragment (file:///data/run#1), a URL without a path (file:) and a percent-encoding that is not valid UTF-8 (file:///a%ff) raise a ValueError: no part of a URL is dropped silently.
  • Any other URL, such as s3://bucket/key or http://host/path, raises a ValueError: it is not a local path. For a local directory of that name, write ./s3:/bucket/key.
  • In a file: URL, write a ? of a file name as %3F and a # as %23, or give the path without file:.
  • Any other string is a plain path, written as is: /data/a?b, /data/run#1 and /data/a%20b keep the ?, the # and the %20. A colon is allowed (a:b), and so is a Windows drive (C://x), because a scheme has two characters or more here.
  • A pathlib.Path is accepted, so the output of hya.path can be passed to hya.path again.
  • A path with a tilde must be quoted in an interpolation: ${hya.path:"~/data"}. Unquoted, it is a grammar error.
  • A value that is not a string or a path raises a TypeError, and a ~user path of an unknown user raises a RuntimeError.
  • A relative path is resolved against the working directory of the process when the value is accessed. Hydra can change this directory (hydra.job.chdir).

docs.title: hya.iter_join
docs.text:
Joins elements of an iterable into a string with a separator.

Syntax: ${hya.iter_join:iterable,separator}

Example:

# Simple join
joined: ${hya.iter_join:[a,b,c],-} # Result: "a-b-c"

# Build paths
paths:
  root: data
  project: myproject
  version: v1
  full_path: ${hya.iter_join:[${paths.root},${paths.project},${paths.version}],/}
  # Result: "data/myproject/v1"

# Build experiment names
experiment:
  model: resnet
  dataset: cifar10
  name: ${hya.iter_join:[${experiment.model},${experiment.dataset}],_}
  # Result: "resnet_cifar10"

Equivalent Python:

# iterable is the resolved content of the argument, without configuration nodes
value = separator.join(map(str, iterable))

Notes:

  • The interpolations of the iterable are resolved at any depth, and a missing value (???) is an error.
  • Each element is converted with str: with x: [["${a}"], 2] and a: 1, ${hya.iter_join:${x},-} is [1]-2.
  • The resolver is separator.join over the iterable: a string is joined character by character (${hya.iter_join:abc,-} is a-b-c) and a mapping gives its keys joined (use ${oc.dict.values:x} for its values).
  • Quote a separator that holds a comma or a significant space: ${hya.iter_join:[a,b],', '} is a, b.
  • A first argument that is not iterable raises a TypeError, and a separator that is not a string, such as a number, raises an AttributeError.

Use Case: Dynamically constructing file paths, experiment names, or configuration strings.

docs.title: hya.sha256
docs.text:
Computes the SHA-256 hash of the whole content of a value.

Syntax: ${hya.sha256:value}

Example:

hash: ${hya.sha256:mystring}
# Result: "bd3ff47540b31e62d4ca6b07794e5a886b0f655fc322730f26ecd65cc7dd5c90"

experiment:
  config: "resnet50_adam_0.001"
  version_id: ${hya.sha256:${experiment.config}}
  # Generates consistent hash for versioning

model:
  name: resnet
  depth: 50
model_id: ${hya.sha256:${model}} # Changes when a value of model changes

Equivalent Python:

import hashlib
import json
from enum import Enum
from pathlib import PurePath


def encode(value):
    if isinstance(value, (PurePath, Enum)):
        return str(value)
    raise TypeError(f"hya.sha256 cannot hash a value of type {type(value).__name__}")


# value is the resolved content of the argument, without configuration nodes
if not isinstance(value, str):
    value = json.dumps(
        value, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"), allow_nan=False, default=encode
    )
digest = hashlib.sha256(value.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

Notes:

  • The interpolations of the value are resolved at any depth, and a missing value (???) is an error.
  • A string is hashed as is: the result is the one that other SHA-256 tools give for the text.
  • Any other value is hashed from its canonical JSON form (sorted keys, no space, non-ASCII characters escaped as \uXXXX), so the order of the keys of a mapping does not matter.
  • In this form, a path or an enum is written as its string (Color.RED). An enum that is also an int, a float or a str (an IntEnum, a class Name(str, Enum)) is written as its value.
  • A value without a JSON form (an array, a tensor, a data type, a set, bytes) raises a TypeError. Hash the list or the string it is built from. A mapping that mixes key types cannot be sorted and raises too.
  • A non-finite float (nan or inf) has no JSON form: it raises a ValueError. The string nan is hashed as any string.
  • The type of a value is not part of the hash: the string [1] and the list [1] have the same hash, and so do an integer key and the same string key.

Use Case: Creating unique identifiers for experiments, cache keys, or version tracking.

docs.title: Optional Resolvers
docs.text: These resolvers require additional packages to be installed.

docs.title: Braceexpand
docs.text:
Package Required: braceexpand>=0.1.7

Install with: pip install braceexpand

docs.title: hya.braceexpand
docs.text:
Expands brace patterns similar to bash brace expansion.

Syntax: ${hya.braceexpand:pattern}

Example:

# Numeric range
files: ${hya.braceexpand:"file_{1..5}.txt"}
# Returns a list: [file_1.txt, file_2.txt, ..., file_5.txt]

# Choice expansion
configs: ${hya.braceexpand:"config_{train,val,test}.yaml"}
# Returns a list: [config_train.yaml, config_val.yaml, config_test.yaml]

# Nested patterns
paths: ${hya.braceexpand:"data/{2020..2022}/{jan,feb,mar}"}
# Returns a list: [data/2020/jan, data/2020/feb, ..., data/2022/mar]

# The list can be used by another resolver
names: ${hya.iter_join:${hya.braceexpand:"a{1..3}"},-} # Result: "a1-a2-a3"

Notes:

  • Quote the pattern in an interpolation: unquoted, the braces are a grammar error of OmegaConf. Escaping works too (\{1..4\}), but each comma must be escaped as well (a\{1\,2\}), as an unquoted comma separates two arguments.
  • A pattern with unbalanced braces raises a ValueError.
  • The resolver returns a list, not an iterator: it has a length, can be indexed and can be read several times. The whole expansion is built at once.

Reference: braceexpand documentation

docs.title: NumPy
docs.text:
Package Required: numpy>=2.0

Install with: pip install numpy

docs.title: hya.np.array
docs.text:
Converts data to a NumPy array. The optional second argument is the data type, as a string that np.array accepts (a NumPy resolver of the data type is not needed).

Syntax: ${hya.np.array:data} or ${hya.np.array:data,dtype}

Example:

# 1D array
vector: ${hya.np.array:[1,2,3,4,5]}

# 2D array
matrix: ${hya.np.array:[[1,2,3],[4,5,6]]}

# Array with a data type
weights: ${hya.np.array:[1,2,3],float32} # array([1., 2., 3.], dtype=float32)

# Use in configuration
data:
  channel_means: [0.485, 0.456, 0.406]
  mean: ${hya.np.array:${data.channel_means},float32} # array([0.485, 0.456, 0.406], dtype=float32)

Equivalent Python:

import numpy as np

# data is the resolved content of the argument, without configuration nodes
value = np.asarray(data).copy(order="K")
value = np.asarray(data, dtype=dtype).copy(order="K")  # with a dtype

Notes:

  • The interpolations of the data are resolved at any depth, and a missing value (???) is an error.
  • A mapping is converted as NumPy converts a dictionary, to an array of the data type object. Use ${oc.dict.keys:x} or ${oc.dict.values:x} for an array of its keys or of its values.
  • An array and a tensor (on the CPU and without gradient) are accepted. They are copied: the result does not share memory with them.
  • An unknown data type raises a TypeError, and data that cannot be converted (nested lists of different lengths, a string with a numeric data type) raise a ValueError.

docs.title: PyTorch
docs.text:
Package Required: torch>=2.4

Install with: pip install torch

docs.title: hya.torch.tensor
docs.text:
Converts data to a PyTorch tensor. The optional second argument is the data type: its name, or a torch.dtype such as the output of hya.torch.dtype.

Syntax: ${hya.torch.tensor:data} or ${hya.torch.tensor:data,dtype}

Example:

# 1D tensor
weights: ${hya.torch.tensor:[0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4]}

# 2D tensor
matrix: ${hya.torch.tensor:[[1,2],[3,4]]}

# Tensor with a data type
mask: ${hya.torch.tensor:[1,0,1],bool} # tensor([ True, False,  True])
scale: ${hya.torch.tensor:[1,2],${hya.torch.dtype:float32}} # tensor([1., 2.])

# Use in model configuration
model:
  default_bias: ${hya.torch.tensor:[0.0,0.0,0.0]}

Equivalent Python:

import torch

# data is the resolved content of the argument, without configuration nodes
value = torch.tensor(data)
value = torch.tensor(data, dtype=dtype)  # with a dtype
# data is a tensor
value = data.detach().to(dtype=data.dtype if dtype is None else dtype, copy=True)
# a dtype given by its name is first converted as hya.torch.dtype does

Notes:

  • The interpolations of the data are resolved at any depth, and a missing value (???) is an error.
  • A tensor is accepted, for example the output of another hya.torch.tensor. It is copied: the result does not share memory with it and does not require a gradient. Without a data type, the copy keeps the data type of the tensor.
  • An unknown data type name raises a ValueError, and so do nested lists of different lengths. Data that PyTorch does not support, such as a string, raise a TypeError.

docs.title: hya.torch.dtype
docs.text:
Creates a PyTorch dtype from its string representation.

Syntax: ${hya.torch.dtype:dtype_name}

Example:

# Common dtypes
float_type: ${hya.torch.dtype:float32}
int_type: ${hya.torch.dtype:int64}
bool_type: ${hya.torch.dtype:bool}

# Use in model configuration
model:
  compute_dtype: ${hya.torch.dtype:float16}
  parameter_dtype: ${hya.torch.dtype:float32}

training:
  use_mixed_precision: true
  amp_dtype: ${hya.torch.dtype:float16}

Available dtypes: Common dtype string names include float, float16, float32, float64, bfloat16, int, int8, int16, int32, int64, uint8, bool, complex64, complex128. The exact available dtypes depend on your PyTorch installation. For a complete list, see the PyTorch dtype documentation.

Equivalent Python:

import torch

value = torch.float32  # for dtype_name="float32"

Note: An unknown name raises a ValueError whose message lists the available dtype names, sorted. Through an interpolation, OmegaConf reports it as an InterpolationResolutionError, as for the error of any other resolver.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: This page lists common errors and their solutions.

docs.title: How Errors Are Reported
docs.text:
An optional resolver is always registered. When its package is missing, the call raises a RuntimeError that says how to install the package. An error raised by a resolver is reported by OmegaConf as an InterpolationResolutionError. The message names the original exception (for example ZeroDivisionError raised while resolving interpolation) and the original exception is in the __context__ chain of the error (__cause__ is None):

import hya
from omegaconf import OmegaConf, errors

try:
    conf = OmegaConf.create({"tensor": "${hya.torch.tensor:[1,2,3]}"})
    print(conf.tensor)
except errors.InterpolationResolutionError as error:
    # Without torch: 'torch' package is required but not installed. ... pip install torch
    print(error)

docs.title: Resolver Not Found
docs.text:
Error: omegaconf.errors.UnsupportedInterpolationType: Unsupported interpolation type hya.xxx

Solution: Make sure you have imported hya:

import hya  # This line is required!
from omegaconf import OmegaConf

docs.title: Optional Dependency Missing
docs.text:
Error:

omegaconf.errors.InterpolationResolutionError: RuntimeError raised while resolving interpolation: 'braceexpand' package is required but not installed

The optional resolvers (hya.braceexpand, hya.np.array, hya.torch.*) are always registered, and need their package when they are called.

Solution: Install the required package:

pip install braceexpand  # or numpy, or torch

docs.title: Resolver Already Registered
docs.text:
Error: RuntimeError: A resolver is already registered for 'my_key'

Solution: Use exist_ok=True to override the resolver of the registry:

@registry.register("my_key", exist_ok=True)
def my_resolver(x):
    return x

Warning: A resolver is already registered in OmegaConf for 'my_key': not replaced.

OmegaConf already has a resolver for each key that the warning lists, and register_resolvers() did not replace them.

Solution: Use registry.register_resolvers(replace=True) to replace them.

docs.title: Invalid Resolver Key
docs.text:
Error: ValueError: Invalid resolver key 'my-key': use names made of letters, digits and _, ...

Solution: Use names joined by dots, for example my_key or my.key.

docs.title: Type Errors in Resolvers
docs.text:
Error: TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'

Solution: Ensure your configuration passes correct types.

Wrong, mixing types:

result: ${hya.add:5,abc}

Correct, same types:

result: ${hya.add:5,10}

docs.title: Circular References
docs.text:
Error: omegaconf.errors.InterpolationResolutionError: Recursive interpolation detected

Solution: Avoid self-referential configurations.

Wrong, a circular reference:

x: ${hya.add:${y},1}
y: ${hya.add:${x},1}

Correct, no circular dependency:

x: 5
y: ${hya.add:${x},1}

docs.title: Grammar Error
docs.text:
Error: omegaconf.errors.GrammarParseError: token recognition error at: '~'

Solution: Quote an argument that holds a special character:

home: ${hya.path:"~/data"}

docs.title: Unquoted Brace Pattern
docs.text:
Error: TypeError raised while resolving interpolation: braceexpand_resolver() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given

An unquoted comma separates two arguments, even between escaped braces.

Solution: Quote the pattern:

files: ${hya.braceexpand:"file_{a,b}.txt"}

docs.title: Missing Colon
docs.text:
Error: omegaconf.errors.InterpolationKeyError: Interpolation key 'hya.pi' not found

Without a colon, ${hya.pi} is a reference to the key pi of a section hya.

Solution: Add the colon: ${hya.pi:}.

docs.title: Hydra on Python 3.14
docs.text:
Error: ValueError: badly formed help string, raised by an application decorated with @hydra.main.

This error comes from hydra-core 1.3.8 on Python 3.14, not from hya.

Solution: Use Python 3.11 to 3.13 with this Hydra release.

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text: This guide explains how to use hya in a configuration and in Python. See also Resolvers for each resolver, Custom Resolvers to add your own, Using with Hydra and Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Importing and Automatic Registration
docs.text:
When you import hya, all default resolvers are automatically registered with OmegaConf:

import hya
from omegaconf import OmegaConf

# Resolvers are now available
conf = OmegaConf.create({"result": "${hya.add:2,3}"})
print(conf.result)  # Output: 5

Importing hya is needed once per process, in any module that runs before the values are accessed.

The optional resolvers (hya.braceexpand, hya.np.array, hya.torch.tensor, hya.torch.dtype) are always registered, so the registry has the same keys on every machine. import hya does not import numpy, torch or braceexpand: the module of an optional resolver is imported on the first call of that resolver, which raises an error that says how to install the package if it is missing.

docs.title: Using Resolvers in YAML Configurations
docs.text:
You can use resolvers directly in YAML configuration files:

# config.yaml
model:
  layers: 4
  hidden_size: 256
  # NOTE: This is a simple demonstration of the mul resolver
  # Real neural network parameter counts are much more complex
  approx_params: ${hya.mul:${model.layers},${model.hidden_size}}

training:
  total_samples: 10000
  batch_size: 32
  num_batches: ${hya.ceildiv:${training.total_samples},${training.batch_size}}
  learning_rate: ${hya.pow:10,-3} # 10^-3 = 0.001

Load and use the configuration:

import hya
from omegaconf import OmegaConf

conf = OmegaConf.load("config.yaml")
print(conf.model.approx_params)  # Output: 1024
print(conf.training.num_batches)  # Output: 313
print(conf.training.learning_rate)  # Output: 0.001

docs.title: Interpolation Syntax
docs.text:
A resolver is called with ${key:argument1,argument2,...}. The syntax is the one of OmegaConf; hya adds the resolvers only. The following rules cover the common cases.

x: 4
# A reference is an argument like any other
double: ${hya.mul:${x},2} # 8
# Calls can be nested
nested: ${hya.add:${hya.mul:${x},3},1} # 13
# The colon is required, even without argument
tau: ${hya.mul:2,${hya.pi:}} # 6.283185307179586
# An interpolation can be a part of a string
name: run-${hya.add:${x},1} # "run-5"
# Numbers, booleans and null are typed; a quoted value is a string
number: ${hya.add:1,2} # 3
text: ${hya.add:'1','2'} # "12"
# Lists and dictionaries can be written in the arguments
length: ${hya.len:[1,2,3]} # 3
# Quote a string that holds a comma or a space that matters
joined: ${hya.iter_join:[a,b],', '} # "a, b"
# Quote a string that holds a special character, such as ~, =, { or }
home: ${hya.path:"~/data"}
# A backslash keeps the text as is
literal: \${hya.add:1,2} # "${hya.add:1,2}"

Spaces around the arguments are ignored. A resolver is called with positional arguments only.

In a Python string, write the interpolation as is ("${hya.add:1,2}"); do not use an f-string, which would read the braces. In YAML, quote a whole value that holds a colon followed by a space, or a space followed by a #, as for any YAML string.

docs.title: Using the Values in Python
docs.text:
Accessing a key calls the resolver and returns its output, which can be any Python object:

import hya
from omegaconf import OmegaConf

conf = OmegaConf.create({"output": "${hya.path:/data/output}", "steps": "${hya.add:1,2}"})
print(conf.output.name)  # Output: output
print(conf.steps + 1)  # Output: 4

To get a plain dictionary with the resolved values, use OmegaConf.to_container:

import hya
from omegaconf import OmegaConf

conf = OmegaConf.create({"model": {"size": "${hya.mul:64,4}"}})
print(OmegaConf.to_container(conf, resolve=True))  # Output: {'model': {'size': 256}}

An array, a tensor or a data type is not a value that a configuration can store. to_container returns it, but OmegaConf.resolve, which replaces the interpolations in place, needs the allow_objects flag, and OmegaConf.to_yaml(conf, resolve=True) does not support it:

import hya
from omegaconf import OmegaConf, flag_override

conf = OmegaConf.create({"dtype": "${hya.torch.dtype:float32}"})
with flag_override(conf, "allow_objects", True):
    OmegaConf.resolve(conf)
print(conf.dtype)  # Output: torch.float32

OmegaConf.to_yaml(conf), without resolve=True, writes the interpolations as they are, so use it to save a configuration.

docs.title: Path Construction
docs.text:
Build file paths dynamically:

paths:
  root: /data
  project: myproject
  version: v1

  # Build paths using iter_join
  data_dir: ${hya.iter_join:[${paths.root},${paths.project},${paths.version}],/}
  train_file: ${hya.iter_join:[${paths.data_dir},train.csv],/}

  # Use path resolver for proper Path objects
  model_checkpoint: ${hya.path:${paths.data_dir}/models/checkpoint.pth}

  # A tilde must be quoted in an interpolation (unquoted, it is a grammar error)
  home_dir: ${hya.path:"~/data"}

docs.title: Mathematical Computations
docs.text:
Perform calculations in your configuration:

model:
  embedding_dim: 512
  num_heads: 8
  head_dim: ${hya.floordiv:${model.embedding_dim},${model.num_heads}} # 64

training:
  total_steps: 100000
  warmup_ratio: 0.1
  # 100000 * 0.1 is the float 10000.0: cast it back to an integer with hya.int
  warmup_steps: ${hya.int:${hya.mul:${training.total_steps},${training.warmup_ratio}}} # 10000

  # Calculate batch size for distributed training
  per_device_batch_size: 16
  num_devices: 4
  global_batch_size: ${hya.mul:${training.per_device_batch_size},${training.num_devices}}

docs.title: Data Type Specifications (PyTorch)
docs.text:
Specify tensor data types in configuration:

model:
  dtype: ${hya.torch.dtype:float32}
  use_half_precision: false
  compute_dtype: ${hya.torch.dtype:float16}

data:
  class_weights: [1, 2, 5]
  weights: ${hya.torch.tensor:${data.class_weights}} # tensor([1, 2, 5])
  # The data type is the second argument of the tensor resolver: its name or a torch.dtype
  float_weights: ${hya.torch.tensor:${data.class_weights},float32} # tensor([1., 2., 5.])
  same_dtype_weights: ${hya.torch.tensor:${data.class_weights},${model.dtype}}

The NumPy resolver takes the data type as a string too: ${hya.np.array:[1,2,3],float32}.

docs.title: Versioning and Hashing
docs.text:
Generate consistent identifiers:

experiment:
  model_name: resnet50
  dataset: imagenet
  augmentation: heavy

  # Create a unique experiment ID
  full_name: ${experiment.model_name}_${experiment.dataset}_${experiment.augmentation}
  experiment_id: ${hya.sha256:${experiment.full_name}}

  # Use for reproducible paths
  output_dir: ${hya.iter_join:[outputs,${experiment.experiment_id}],/}

model:
  name: resnet
  depth: 50
model_id: ${hya.sha256:${model}} # The hash of the whole section

hya.sha256 hashes the resolved content of a value: a string as is, any other value as canonical JSON, so the order of the keys does not matter. A value without a JSON form, such as an array, a tensor or a non-finite float, raises an error. See hya.sha256.

docs.title: List Operations
docs.text:
Work with lists and sequences:

datasets:
  train: [mnist, cifar10, imagenet]
  num_datasets: ${hya.len:${datasets.train}}

  # Join dataset names
  combined_name: ${hya.iter_join:${datasets.train},_} # mnist_cifar10_imagenet

docs.title: Brace Expansion (requires braceexpand)
docs.text:
Generate multiple values from patterns:

files:
  # Expands to a list: file_1.txt, file_2.txt, ..., file_5.txt
  pattern: ${hya.braceexpand:"file_{1..5}.txt"}

  # Expands to a list: train_a.json, train_b.json, train_c.json
  train_configs: ${hya.braceexpand:"train_{a,b,c}.json"}

The pattern must be quoted in an interpolation. The result is a list (it has a length, can be indexed and can be read several times), so it can be used by other resolvers such as hya.iter_join.

docs.title: Working with Complex Data Types
docs.text:
Create NumPy arrays and PyTorch tensors:

import hya
from omegaconf import OmegaConf

conf = OmegaConf.create(
    {
        "numpy_array": "${hya.np.array:[[1,2,3],[4,5,6]]}",
        "torch_tensor": "${hya.torch.tensor:[1.0,2.0,3.0]}",
        "torch_dtype": "${hya.torch.dtype:float32}",
    }
)

print(type(conf.numpy_array))  # <class 'numpy.ndarray'>
print(type(conf.torch_tensor))  # <class 'torch.Tensor'>
print(conf.torch_dtype)  # torch.float32

docs.title: Combining Multiple Resolvers
docs.text:
Chain resolvers for complex operations:

model:
  base_size: 64
  multiplier: 4
  layers: 3

  # Compute total size: (64 * 4) * 3 = 768
  intermediate_size: ${hya.mul:${model.base_size},${model.multiplier}}
  total_size: ${hya.mul:${model.intermediate_size},${model.layers}}

docs.title: Using Resolvers with OmegaConf Features
docs.text:
Combine resolvers with OmegaConf's native features:

# Use resolvers with the oc.env resolver of OmegaConf
paths:
  root: /data
  project: ${oc.env:PROJECT_NAME,default_project}
  output: ${hya.iter_join:[${paths.root},${paths.project}],/}

# Use resolvers with Hydra overrides
model:
  size: 512 # Can be overridden via the command line: model.size=1024
  doubled_size: ${hya.mul:${model.size},2}

docs.title: Configuration Organization
docs.text:
Organize your configurations for maintainability:

# Good: Use resolvers to avoid duplication
model:
  hidden_size: 768
  num_layers: 12
  total_hidden: ${hya.mul:${model.hidden_size},${model.num_layers}}

# Avoid: Hardcoding computed values
# total_hidden: 9216  # If you change hidden_size, this becomes incorrect

docs.title: Type Safety
docs.text:
Use appropriate resolvers for type safety:

# Good: Use correct division operators
samples: 1000
batch_size: 32
num_batches: ${hya.ceildiv:${samples},${batch_size}} # Integer result: 32

# Avoid: Using wrong division type
# num_batches: ${hya.truediv:${samples},${batch_size}}  # Float result: 31.25

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
Resolvers are evaluated lazily when accessed:

conf = OmegaConf.create(
    {"slow_computation": "${hya.pow:2,1000}", "fast_value": 42}  # Not computed yet
)

# Only computed when accessed
result = conf.slow_computation  # Computed here

OmegaConf does not cache the output of a resolver: every access of an interpolation calls the resolver again, even when several keys point to the same interpolation. Compute an expensive value once in Python and store it in the configuration if it is used many times:

model:
  vocab_size: 50000
  embedding_dim: 512
  total_embeddings: ${hya.mul:${model.vocab_size},${model.embedding_dim}}

layer1:
  input_size: ${model.total_embeddings} # Calls hya.mul at each access

layer2:
  input_size: ${model.total_embeddings} # Calls hya.mul at each access

docs.title: Main functions
docs.text: The package, the resolver registry and the default registry. See Custom Resolvers to learn how to use them.

docs.title: hya
docs.text:
Contain the main features of the hya package.

Importing hya publishes the default resolvers to OmegaConf, so a configuration can use them without any other call. The package exposes ResolverRegistry and get_default_registry to add your own resolvers.

Example 
>>> import hya
>>> from omegaconf import OmegaConf
>>> conf = OmegaConf.create({"steps": "${hya.ceildiv:1000,32}"})
>>> conf.steps
32

docs.title: hya.ResolverRegistry
docs.text:
Implement a resolver registry.

A registry maps keys to resolvers. register and register_lazy add a resolver to the registry, and register_resolvers publishes the registry to OmegaConf, so that configurations can use the keys. A registry is independent of the other registries.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default state Mapping[str, Callable[..., Any]] | None

Optional initial state mapping containing key-resolver pairs, or None for an empty registry. A copy is made to prevent external modifications. Each pair is added with register, so it is validated.

None

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

If state is not a mapping or None, if a key of state is not a string, or if a value is not callable.

ValueError

If a key of state is not made of names joined by dots (see register).

Example 
>>> from omegaconf import OmegaConf
>>> from hya.registry import ResolverRegistry
>>> registry = ResolverRegistry({"demo.upper": str.upper})
>>> @registry.register("demo.double")
... def double_resolver(value):
...     return value * 2
...
>>> registry.register_resolvers()
>>> conf = OmegaConf.create({"x": "${demo.double:4}", "y": "${demo.upper:abc}"})
>>> conf.x, conf.y
(8, 'ABC')

docs.title: hya.ResolverRegistry.state property
docs.text:
state: Mapping[str, Callable[..., Any]]

The state of the registry.

This is a read-only view: use register to add a resolver.

Example 
>>> from hya.registry import ResolverRegistry
>>> registry = ResolverRegistry()
>>> @registry.register("my_key")
... def my_resolver(value):
...     return value
...
>>> list(registry.state)
['my_key']

docs.title: hya.ResolverRegistry.has_resolver
docs.text:
has_resolver(key: str) -> bool

Check if a resolver is explicitly registered for the given key.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default key str

The key to check.

required

Returns:

Type Description bool

True if a resolver is registered for this key,

bool

False otherwise

Example 
>>> from hya.registry import ResolverRegistry
>>> registry = ResolverRegistry()
>>> @registry.register("my_key")
... def my_resolver(value):
...     pass
...
>>> registry.has_resolver("my_key")
True
>>> registry.has_resolver("missing")
False

docs.title: hya.ResolverRegistry.register
docs.text:
register(
    key: str, *, exist_ok: bool = False
) -> Callable[[F], F]

Register a resolver to registry with the specified key.

This method returns a decorator that can be used to register resolver functions.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default key str

The key used to register the resolver: names made of ASCII letters, digits and _ that do not start with a digit, joined by dots (for example "my.resolver_2"). Every supported OmegaConf can interpolate such a key. Must be unique unless exist_ok is True.

required exist_ok bool

If False, a RuntimeError is raised if you try to register a new resolver with an existing key. If True, the existing resolver will be overridden.

False

Returns:

Type Description Callable[[F], F]

A decorator function that registers the resolver and returns it unchanged.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

If the key is not a string (for example @registry.register used without a key), or if the resolver is not callable.

ValueError

If the key is not made of names joined by dots.

RuntimeError

If the key already exists and exist_ok is False.

Example 
>>> from hya.registry import ResolverRegistry
>>> registry = ResolverRegistry()
>>> @registry.register("my_key")
... def my_resolver(value):
...     return value * 2
...
>>> my_resolver(5)
10

docs.title: hya.ResolverRegistry.register_lazy
docs.text:
register_lazy(
    key: str, target: str, *, exist_ok: bool = False
) -> None

Register a resolver that is imported on its first call.

The module of the resolver is not imported when the resolver is registered, but the first time OmegaConf calls the resolver.
